analysis.one_liner: Charges opioid drug makers up to $2 billion a year for ten years to fund addiction treatment.
analysis.headline: The bill was never considered: it sat in the Senate health committee with no cosponsors and no action until the 2019-2020 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Department of Health and Human Services to charge prescription opioid manufacturers an annual fee, totaling $2 billion a year, split among companies according to their share of the opioid market. Companies would pay it for ten years, and opioids made to treat addiction, cancer pain, or hospice care would be exempt. All the money would go to the existing federal block grant that funds state and local substance abuse prevention and treatment programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic, and the state and local treatment and prevention programs that the federal block grant supports. People with opioid use disorder would gain access to more treatment services without new taxes on ordinary taxpayers, since the fee falls on drug manufacturers instead.

how_it_helps.text: Fees of $2 billion a year for ten years would flow into the Substance Abuse Prevention and Treatment block grant, the main federal funding stream for state and community addiction treatment and prevention services.
The fee is set by each manufacturer's share of the opioid market, so the companies that sold the most opioids pay the most.
Drugs used to treat opioid addiction, cancer pain, or hospice care are excluded from the fee, so treatment medications themselves are not taxed.
The money is transferred to HHS specifically for the block grant program, so the funding has a dedicated use.

analysis.who_pays: Prescription opioid manufacturers, including the large pharmaceutical companies that produced opioid painkillers since 1999, would pay up to $2 billion a year for a decade, apportioned by market share. Some of that cost could be passed through to patients and payers through higher drug prices.

drawbacks.text: Companies facing a $2 billion annual fee could raise prices on opioid painkillers, raising costs for legitimate pain patients, though drugs for cancer, hospice, and addiction treatment are exempt.

The fee is imposed on manufacturers for activity dating back to 1999 regardless of any individual finding of wrongdoing, which invites legal challenges and would almost certainly draw years of litigation from the industry.
The funding lasts only ten years, so after the fee expires, communities that built treatment programs around the money would face a funding cliff.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A decade of $2 billion in dedicated addiction treatment funding, paid by the companies that dominated the opioid market rather than by taxpayers, is a substantial benefit for communities dealing with the epidemic. The main risks are price pass-through to pain patients, an industry legal fight over the fee, and the funding ending after ten years. On balance the design is straightforward and the benefit outweighs the acknowledged costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the Opioid Treatment Surge Act in the Senate on May 23, 2019.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No cosponsors signed on to the bill.
No further action was ever taken on the bill, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid manufacturers kept the roughly $2 billion a year in fees they would have owed, and the treatment programs the bill would have funded never received it.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never took it up; no hearing, markup, or vote occurred before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors and no votes ever recorded the chamber's position, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would charge companies that have made opioid drugs since 1999 up to $2 billion a year, split by market share, to fund treatment. Their interest in avoiding the fee runs directly against the public's interest in funded addiction treatment.

Their drugs (for example buprenorphine and methadone used in treatment) are exempt from the fee, and expanded block grant funding would grow the market for addiction treatment services. They gain from the treatment surge without paying the fee.

industries.industry: Community mental health and substance abuse treatment providers
industries.note: The block grant that funds state and community treatment and prevention programs would receive $2 billion a year in new dedicated funding.
